chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys a camel (for Hajj sacrifice), then it gets lost before he marks it and puts a ring in its nose, so he does not find it until he arrives at Mina, so he slaughters (another one), and he finds his sacrifice (the lost one). He said: 'If he had not yet marked it, it is from his wealth; if he wishes, he slaughters it, and if he wishes, he sells it. And if he had marked it, he slaughters it.' And whoever loses his sacrifice, and another finds it and slaughters it on his behalf, if he slaughters it at Mina, it suffices for him, and if he slaughters it elsewhere, it does not suffice for him. Narrated.

key_terms.مِنًى: Mina, a location near Mecca where sacrifices are performed
key_terms.يَشْعَرَهَا: To mark the animal (typically by cutting hair)
key_terms.يُقَلِّدَهَا: To put a ring in the nose of the animal

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim's sacrificial camel is lost and found by someone else?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the status of the *badanah* (large sacrificial animal) based on whether it has been marked (*ash'ara*), distinguishing between personal property rights and ritual obligation. It further establishes the geographic validity of the sacrifice, ruling that if a finder slaughters the lost animal, it is only valid if done within the specific precincts of Mina, reflecting the strict spatial requirements of Hajj rituals.
